Won the intern hackathon at T-Mobile last week alongside my partner, Cooper Hampton . Our team built a full-stack AI benefits navigator to help disabled veterans access the resources they're entitled to, and shipped it in 16 hours. I led the technical build: React frontend, FastAPI backend, and a keyword-scoring NLP layer (alias expansion, intent weighting, conversational context resolution) that routes natural-language queries across 15 different benefit domains with no live model dependency. One thing I had to figure out on the fly: I had four Claude Code agents working in parallel to hit our timeline, which meant setting up file-ownership rules upfront so they wouldn't overwrite each other. It worked, we shipped 15+ components without a single merge conflict, but I spent more time thinking about how to coordinate the agents than writing code myself. We also set hard limits on what the tool could and couldn't say. No eligibility determinations, no tax advice, nothing touching protected-class status, everything scoped to draft-only correspondence so we stayed within 38 CFR Part 14. Felt important to get that right given who the tool is actually for. Got the privilege to present the project to and be judged by a panel of T-Mobile Executives, who voted unanimously to award us first place: Chief Legal Officer Mark Nelson Chief Financial Officer Peter Osvaldik Chief Network Officer Ankur Kapoor Chief Data & AI Officer Grant R. VP of Product & Engineering Kevin Lau Special thanks to Taylor Roman and the Emerging Talent Team for organizing this wonderful event across all three locations: Caroline Brock , Brittnie Thompson , Dakota W. , Melissa Van Wey, MA , Nora Smith , Kristen Grover , Danielle Jenkins , Therasa Cha , Spenser Holman , and Sean Lynott, MBA #Hackathon #AI #TMobile

Excited to share that our paper "Comparing Developer and LLM Biases in Code Evaluation" has been accepted to COLM 2026 and the ICML DL4C Workshop! As LLMs are increasingly deployed as judges to evaluate code, a key question remains: Do they actually care about the same things human developers care about? To find out, we introduced TRACE, a framework designed to evaluate LLM judges in realistic, interactive software engineering settings. Key takeaways from our findings: 📉 Alignment Gap: Even the best LLM judges underperform human annotators by 12–23% when predicting developer preferences. 🔍 Systematic Biases: TRACE exposed significant sources of misalignment. For instance, in code completion settings, LLM judges overemphasize functionality, whereas real developers prioritize code clarity. 🛠️ Code Quality Mismatch: The majority of these misalignments map directly to standard software engineering code quality criteria where models and humans weigh priorities completely differently. Huge thank you to Ryan Shar for his collaboration throughout this project! Also deeply grateful to Valerie Chen and Wayne Chi for their guidance, and my collaborators Zichu Wu and Shyam Agarwal . Check out the full preprint on arXiv if you're interested in LLM evaluation in code settings: https://lnkd.in/gD_FDKW9
